problem: Existing VLN surveys taxonomize the field only by learning method or by task type, and none gives a unified view covering core concepts, datasets and simulators, applications, comparative analysis, and challenges together.
motivation: VLN has grown quickly, and its contributions are fragmented across frameworks, models, auxiliary modules, tasks, datasets and simulators. A unified layered taxonomy makes strengths and weaknesses comparable, exposes research gaps, and helps researchers target specific sub-problems on the way to home-assistant robots.
key_idea: Organize VLN literature into a four-layer abstraction (frameworks, models, auxiliaries, tasks), compare works within each layer, and consolidate datasets, simulators and open challenges.
insight: The review argues that the main bottlenecks are generalization to unseen environments, continuous-environment navigation (long action sequences, collisions, no backtracking), mapless agents, and sim-to-real transfer. Model categories are compared only qualitatively and through a chart (Fig. 7) of average SR/SPL/NE by category, where graph-based models are strongest, followed by memory-based and hybrid. Graph-based models are tied to discrete graphs and pre-exploration, while hybrid models mostly stay below 50% SPL. Only four works have real-robot deployments, and most models are trained on short R2R trajectories.
method: Four-layer taxonomy: frameworks (modular vs end-to-end), models, auxiliaries (approaches + modules) and tasks, each with sub-classes (Fig. 4-5).
Model classification: graph-based, generative, memory-based, reasoning and hybrid models, compared on strengths and weaknesses (Table 2).
Auxiliaries: approaches (sub-goals, pre-exploration, adversarial attacks) and modules (trajectory scoring, progress monitors, perception modules, etc.).
Learning methods: representational learning, RL, zero-shot, and limited-data methods (augmentation, transfer, meta-learning, pre-training, auxiliary tasks, self-supervised, curriculum).
Resource consolidation: table of 23 datasets (Table 5), 8 simulators (Tables 6-7), and a discussion of real-robot deployments.
Challenge and future-direction analysis: generalization, VLN-CE, mapless navigation, backtracking in continuous settings, LLMs, multisensory grounding, dynamic and aerial tasks.

setting.simulator: n/a (reviews Matterport3D, Habitat, AI2-Thor, Gibson, House3D, VizDoom, AerialVLN, Sim-to-Real)

numbers_note: Survey paper with no new experimental results; the only performance comparison is a qualitative chart (Fig. 7) of average metrics per model category.
results: The survey finds graph-based models perform best on average, followed by memory-based and hybrid models; reasoning and generative models are weaker. It reports low SR/SPL in unseen environments, long-horizon degradation on R4R, and only four real-world VLN deployments (Sim-to-Real, LM-Nav, CA-Nav and [202]). It identifies generalization, continuous navigation, sim-to-real transfer and backtracking in continuous settings as key open problems.
limitations: Coverage of LLM/VLM-based and foundation-model VLN (e.g. NavGPT-style agents, video/VLA models) is thin, and there is no quantitative results table across methods.
Taxonomy boundaries are fuzzy (e.g. hybrid vs reasoning models), and the survey has no systematic search protocol or paper counts.
Some claims are asserted without evidence, such as that backtracking has been applied only to discrete settings and that graph-based models have not been adapted to continuous ones.
builds_on: Existing VLN surveys (Gu et al. 2022, Wu et al. 2023, Zhang et al. 2024)
